input: The inventory policy adopted for the spare motor provides for a safety stock of 602 units, a level that has been set so as to deliver a 95% cycle service level across the full replenishment lead time. The underlying demand pattern is characterised by a mean demand of 526 units per week, with a standard deviation of weekly demand amounting to 129 units, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. For the purposes of the calculation, weekly demand is treated as following a normal distribution, and demand arising in any given week is treated as statistically independent of the demand arising in any other week. It should be emphasised that the safety stock exists to absorb the variability that accumulates over the lead time, rather than the average demand itself, which is covered by the replenishment quantity. It is also important to note that seasonal peaks have been excluded from the demand history on which the calculation is based, so the 602 units cannot be relied upon to sustain the service level through a lead time falling in a peak season. The buffer will be maintained at this level for as long as the demand record and the lead time remain unchanged; should either the lead time lengthen or the spread of weekly demand widen, the required stock will be recalculated accordingly.
target: Safety stock for the spare motor is 602 units, which gives a 95% cycle service level over the replenishment lead time. Mean demand is 526 units per week, and the standard deviation of weekly demand is 129 units. The replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. Weekly demand is treated as normal, and demand in one week is treated as independent of demand in any other week. The stock covers the variation in demand that accumulates over the lead time under that pattern; it is not sized for the average demand itself, which the replenishment quantity covers. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record behind the calculation. The 602 units therefore do not cover a lead time that falls in a peak season, and a policy that must hold service through the peaks needs a separate seasonal allowance. The buffer is held at the stated level while the demand record and the lead time stand. A longer lead time, or a wider spread in weekly demand, raises the stock that the same service level requires, and the figure is recalculated when either changes. Stock drawn below the safety level is cover consumed by variation, and it is restored by the next replenishment rather than treated as available for planned issues.
